challenges.name: coupling-cohesion-quiz
challenges.title: What do fan-in and fan-out tell you?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the utils incident: the coupling report of the API's modules, and which modules use which export of utils.

questions.question:
The coupling report of the CodeDev API, run the day after a one-line change to formatDate() in utils broke 9 features:

module          fanIn  fanOut  instability
utils               9       0         0.00
catalog             3       2         0.40
payments            2       2         0.50
notifications       2       1         0.33
orders              1       5         0.83
progress            1       3         0.75

Statement: "utils has an instability of 0.00, so it is the safest module to change: nothing it depends on can break it."
questions.explanation: False. Instability = fanOut / (fanIn + fanOut). A value of 0 means the module depends on nothing and many modules depend on it: it will rarely be broken by others, but every change to it reaches all 9 importers, which is exactly what happened. "Stable" in this metric means hard to change safely, not safe to change. A module like this needs a small, deliberate API and tests that cover its callers before any edit; orders (0.83) is the one that can change cheaply, because only 1 module depends on it. The misconception is reading "stable" as "low risk".

questions.question:
Which modules import which export of src/utils/index.ts (from a search of the import lines):

export           imported by
formatPrice      catalog, orders, payments
formatDate       catalog, orders, progress, notifications
sendEmail        notifications, orders
calculateLevel   progress, leaderboard
slugify          catalog

The proposal: replace utils with three modules, money (formatPrice), email (sendEmail) and levels (calculateLevel); formatDate and slugify move to a small text module.

Statement: "After this split, a change to calculateLevel can break progress and leaderboard, but it can no longer break catalog or orders."
questions.explanation: True. After the split, only progress and leaderboard import levels, so a change to calculateLevel reaches exactly those two; catalog and orders import money and text, which did not change. Each new module is also more cohesive: everything in it changes for the same reason (pricing rules, email delivery, the level formula). Before the split, every importer of utils depended on all five functions at once, so any edit touched all of them. The misconception is that splitting a module only moves code around: it changes who depends on what, which is what decides how far a change spreads.

challenges.name: measure-module-coupling
challenges.title: Measure coupling: fan-in, fan-out and instability
challenges.description: A one-line change to the shared utils module of the CodeDev API broke 9 features in one release, and nobody knew how many modules depended on it. Write analyzeCoupling(edges, limits) to turn the module dependency graph into numbers. Each edge is a string "a -> b" (module a imports module b); spaces around the arrow are optional. A line is valid when it contains exactly one "->" and each side, after trimming, is one non-empty module name without whitespace; count invalid lines in skipped and ignore them otherwise. The same edge listed twice counts once. A self-edge ("a -> a") adds no dependency, but every module named in a valid line appears in the report. fanIn = how many other modules import the module; fanOut = how many other modules it imports. instability = Math.round(fanOut * 100 / (fanIn + fanOut)) / 100, and 0 when fanIn + fanOut is 0. flags, in this order: "high-fan-in" when fanIn > limits.maxFanIn, "high-fan-out" when fanOut > limits.maxFanOut, otherwise an empty array. Sort the modules by fanIn (highest first), then fanOut (highest first), then name A to Z (compared with < and >). Return { modules: [{ module, fanIn, fanOut, instability, flags }], skipped }. The test runner reads { edges, limits } as JSON from stdin and prints the report as JSON. Up to a few thousand edges.
hints: Fan-in counts distinct importers, not import lines. What data structure keeps one entry per importer even when the same edge appears three times with different spacing?

Work in three passes: parse and validate each line (split on "->", trim both sides, check the number of parts and that no name is empty or contains whitespace), record the module names and the edges, then build one report row per module and sort. The self-edge check comes after a module has been recorded, not before.

A similar graph: "lessons -> media", "quizzes->media", "lessons -> media", "media -> cdn", "cdn -> cdn", "media cdn". One line is invalid (skipped 1). media is imported by lessons and quizzes (fanIn 2) and imports cdn (fanOut 1): instability = Math.round(100 / 3) / 100 = 0.33. cdn: fanIn 1, fanOut 0, instability 0. lessons and quizzes: fanIn 0, fanOut 1, instability 1. Order: media, cdn, then lessons before quizzes.

tests.name: The incident graph: utils is imported by every feature module
Duplicates and spacing count once, a self-edge adds nothing, a bad line is skipped
Limits: a count equal to the limit is not flagged; one module gets both flags
Invalid lines (no arrow, two arrows, empty side, => arrow, a name with a space) are skipped
Rounding 1/3, 2/3 and 1/8 to two decimals; a module with only a self-edge has instability 0
Only blank lines: no modules, every line skipped
Large graph: 303 modules, 2,600 lines with duplicates, self-edges and bad lines
